repeats.title: Repeats with the music
repeats.text: For every click in the music the analysis looks for the same music (±200 ms of treble envelope) within ±8 s. If the same hit sits there as well, the click repeats: a sequenced drum hit comes back bar after bar, a defect does not. The number is how often it came back.
repeats.more: Hits every revolution are excluded, that is a scratch. Music that does not loop (rock, jazz, classical) typically shows 1–4 % repeating clicks, a drum machine 50 % and more.
repeat_rule.title: Sequenced music
repeat_rule.text: Electronic music is hard for any click detector: a drum-computer hit looks exactly like a click. From 20 % repeating clicks in the music on, the recording counts as sequenced and the repeating clicks are left out of the count and the grade (“automatic”). Per record you can switch the rule on or off for good. Without a choice of your own, the default follows the record's Discogs genres and styles: Hip Hop and the beat-based styles of Electronic (Techno, House, Electro, Synth-pop, EBM, Trance, Drum n Bass …) on, Classical off, everything else automatic.
repeat_rule.more: Your verdicts always win: “click” on a repeating hit counts it again, “false alarm” on any click takes it out. The share and the number taken out are shown under the event list.
grouping.title: Audible clicks
grouping.text: A particle or a scratch makes the stylus bounce: two or three impulses within 10–20 ms that the ear hears as one click. Impulses within 20 ms of a stronger one are counted with it as one audible click; the list shows the strongest with “×3” and hides the others unless “show single impulses” is on.
grouping.more: Crackle is not grouped, its density is the measure. The turntable baseline from the silent groove of the test record is counted the same way from the next alignment run on.
mono.title: Mono record
mono.text: A mono record carries its signal as lateral groove movement; what differs between left and right is vertical movement, that is noise and damage. Summed to L+R (the mono switch) it cancels, and a true mono cartridge does not read it at all. Analysed this way the same record gets a better and more honest grade for mono playback.
mono.more: Set per record; a new record from a Discogs release marked Mono starts with it on. Switching analyses every side again whose audio is still there. Alignment and calibration recordings are not affected.
grade_calc.title: How the grade is made
grade_calc.text: The grade comes from the clicks and pops per minute in the music (90 %) and, counted once more on their own, the pops per minute (10 %), each on a scale calibrated on cleaned records. The second opinion of the grooveclean network confirms the candidates on every installation, so the same recording gets the same grade on a Raspberry Pi and in the desktop apps. Counted are audible clicks that are neither your false alarms nor, in sequenced music, hits that repeat with the music, nor mechanical shocks (needle drop, dust cover). Quiet passages, crackle and noise are shown for information only.
grade_calc.more: Hover over a grade for the limits of the scale; the explanation under the grade names everything that was taken out.
verdicts.title: Your verdicts
verdicts.text: ▶ listen, then judge. “Click” counts the detection even if the repeat rule took it out, “false alarm” (the music itself) takes it out of count and grade at once, “unsure” leaves it to the rules. Verdicts stay with the place, survive a new analysis and train the station model.
verdicts.more: Most useful to judge: strong clicks without repeats in loud passages (music the rule missed?) and repeating ones in quiet passages (a defect the rule took?).
